analysis.one_liner: Tightens oil spill prevention rules and extends the Gulf of Mexico offshore drilling moratorium.
analysis.headline: The Marine Oil Spill Prevention Act was introduced in the Senate in January 2017 and referred to committee, but never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would extend the ban on new oil and gas leasing in parts of the Gulf of Mexico to June 30, 2027, make owners of oil responsible for spill cleanup regardless of the vessel that carries it, and tighten Coast Guard inspections of tank ships. It would create a citizens' advisory council for the Gulf Coast, funded by the oil and shipping companies it oversees, and require faster public release of spill response plans. It would also fund coastal state spill planning and long-term Gulf environmental monitoring. It never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Gulf Coast residents, beach communities, and people whose jobs depend on clean water — commercial and recreational fishing, restaurants, hotels, and tourism. Coastal states would get grants and better spill planning, and the public would get faster information during any spill.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gulf Coast communities and fishing and tourism businesses

how_it_helps.text: Extends the moratorium on oil and gas leasing in certain Gulf of Mexico areas to June 30, 2027, keeping those waters off-limits to new drilling and the spill risk that comes with it.
Changes the law so the owner of spilled oil is responsible for cleanup in all cases, not just when it is carried in a single-hull vessel.

Creates a Gulf Coast Regional Citizens' Advisory Council — modeled on the citizen council created after the Exxon Valdez — whose voting members represent fishing, tourism, conservation, and local governments, with an up to $10 million annual budget paid by the companies it oversees.
Requires the Coast Guard to publish oil spill Incident Action Plans on a public website within 12 hours of approval, so residents know what responders are doing during a spill.
Authorizes grants of up to $750,000 a year to coastal states to strengthen their own oil spill planning and response, with no state matching requirement.

Directs NOAA to maintain oil spill trajectory modeling, run a 10-year monitoring and research program on the Gulf environment after the Deepwater Horizon spill, and review its own spill-response capacity.

Increases Coast Guard safety inspections of all tank vessels entering U.S. ports and requires updated, Coast Guard-approved response plans using the best available containment technology every five years.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas operators and oil shipping companies, who would face an extended leasing ban, more inspections, inspection fees, stricter safety management rules for drilling units, and funding obligations for the citizens' council. Those costs could be partly passed on to consumers in fuel prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore oil producers and oil shipping companies

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes new fees and compliance costs on offshore operators and shippers, which could be passed through to consumers at the pump [S3].
Extending the leasing moratorium keeps those Gulf areas closed to energy production through mid-2027, which supporters of expanded drilling argue reduces domestic supply [S2].
The citizens' council would be funded by the covered companies themselves — up to $10 million a year in aggregate — which creates a dependency on the industry it is meant to watch [S3].
Several provisions apply only if Congress appropriates the money, such as the coastal state grants, so the help depends on future funding decisions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would put real protections in place for a region that has absorbed major spill damage before — the Deepwater Horizon disaster is the stated backdrop. The costs fall on a specific industry in the form of fees, inspections, and liability, some of which may reach consumers. The design has one notable weak point: the watchdog council is industry-funded. On balance, the protections for coastal economies and ecosystems outweigh the costs, though the bill never got far enough to be debated or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on January 9, 2017, read twice, and sent to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, where it stayed with no hearing, markup, or floor vote through the end of the 115th Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Nelson introduced the bill on January 9, 2017, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the complete action history before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The bill had the sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors, and no other senators signed on in two years.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas operators and oil shipping companies avoided the extended leasing moratorium, inspection fees, stricter safety rules, and liability changes the bill would have imposed; Gulf Coast communities did not receive the added protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil operators and oil shippers

for.name: Sen. Bill Nelson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, which would extend the Gulf drilling moratorium and strengthen spill prevention, preparedness, and response.

against.name: Sen. John Thune
against.role: Chairman, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee the bill was referred to, never brought it to a committee markup or hearing in the two years it sat there.

sides.party_line_note: The only senators attached to the bill were three Democrats; no Senate votes ever occurred, and no Republicans signed on.

industries.note: The bill extends the Gulf leasing moratorium to 2027, imposes inspection fees, requires safety management systems for mobile offshore drilling units, allows NTSB investigations of OCS accidents, and tightens response plan requirements. Its cost is the industry's cost of preventing spills the public otherwise bears.

industries.industry: Oil shippers and tank vessel operators
industries.note: Owners of oil become responsible for cleanup regardless of hull type, and all tank vessels entering U.S. ports face more frequent and comprehensive Coast Guard inspections.

industries.industry: Gulf Coast fishing and tourism businesses
industries.note: Fishing, tourism, and coastal businesses would get a citizens' council representing their interests, spill planning grants, and monitoring of threats to the resources their livelihoods depend on.
The bill creates a formal Coast Guard program to evaluate and validate containment and removal technologies, giving validated methods a path into required response plans.
